titleStmt.title: Chapter 9 — Christianity and the Postmodern Downfall

div.p: As we have seen in Chapter 7, the spread of universal monotheism starts with a declaration of war against the E-Anna, personified as the Whore of Babylon (Section 7.1.3). As the expectation of the eschaton receded into the far future, this war was internalized.

div.head: 9.1 Augustine — The Internalization of the Kullaba
div.p: Throughout ancient history, the dual sovereignty engine operated strictly as an external, macro-political architecture. The E-Anna was a literal warband and a physical sovereign; the Kullaba was a literal priesthood, a Senate, or a code of laws carved in stone. Christianity’s ultimate civilizational breakthrough was the radical internalization of this entire thermodynamic structure. It achieved what no previous paradigm could: it relocated the Kullaba from the civic square into the individual human psyche.

This psychological revolution is most clearly articulated by Augustine of Hippo. In the City of God,Augustine of Hippo, The City of God against the Pagans, trans. R. W. Dyson (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998), Book XIV, ch. 28. Augustine famously contrasts the City of God, built on the love of God to the contempt of self, with the Earthly City, built on the love of self to the contempt of God—a society entirely driven by the libido dominandi. Augustine definitively unmasks the E-Anna drive—the Roman imperial obsession with martial-erotic glory—as the libido dominandi (the lust for domination). To counteract this, Augustine does not merely propose a better set of external laws; through the Confessions,Augustine of Hippo, Confessions, trans. Henry Chadwick (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1991), Book X. In Book X, Augustine meticulously dissects the mechanisms of memory, temptation, and the concupiscence of the flesh, effectively writing the manual for internal Christian self-surveillance. he engineers a far more effective technology of introspective policing. The individual is trained to relentlessly interrogate their own desires, identifying the mimetic pull of the Ishtarian flesh and subordinating it to the supreme, internal gaze of the Divine Father. The coalition of the meek is no longer just a demographic mass federated by priests; it becomes the default psychological posture of the Christian soul submitting to grace and cemented by agape—that is to say, by the primal social-mammal cohesion instinct.For the biological and evolutionary basis of this primal cohesion instinct—which theology articulates as agape—see Frans de Waal, Primates and Philosophers: How Morality Evolved (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2006). De Waal demonstrates that human moral and cooperative behavior is deeply rooted in the evolutionary biology of social mammals, functioning precisely to bind communities against disruptive, localized aggression. By writing the law on the heart, Christianity effectively installed a miniature, self-sustaining Kullaba inside every believer.

div.head: 9.2 Porneiomachia — The Internalized War on the E-Anna
div.p: This radical internalization did not merely establish an internal tribunal; it declared a state of total, perpetual internal warfare against the BDMB archetype itself—a phenomenon we term porneiomachia (the war against porneia, or sexual-spiritual idolatrous transgression). As this framework has demonstrated, the historical trajectory of the E-Anna is one of gradual structural quarantine. In Late Chalcolithic Uruk and under Sargon (Sections 5.1 and 5.2), the martial-erotic engine was overtly celebrated. By the Augustan synthesis (Section 6.5), it was forced into the quasi-black, operating covertly beneath an Apollonian facade. The biblical prophetic tradition (Section 7.1) aggressively unmasked this covert idol as the Whore of Babylon. During the High Middle Ages (Section 8.2), the Ishtarian drive mutated into the stealth religion of courtly love, retreating into the supposedly neutral sphere of secular entertainment.

The genius of the early Christian ascetics and theologians was recognizing that as long as the erotic component—the porneia—remained active, the charismatic gravity of the BDMB could always resurrect itself. Therefore, the heavily criticized anti-sex and ascetic features of historical Christianity are not expressions of arbitrary patriarchal prudery. They represent a highly sophisticated yet partially unconsciousWithin Christian theology, this semi-unconscious, internalized drive toward orthopraxy, moral self-correction, and communal cohesion is explicitly identified as the operation of the Holy Spirit (the Paraclete). From a sociological and thermodynamic perspective, the Holy Spirit functions as the autonomous, distributed software of the internal Kullaba. socio-psychological strategy: the systematic dismantling of the E-Anna's thermodynamic core. By waging porneiomachia, the internal Kullaba starves the martial-erotic engine of its mimetic fuel, neutralizing the contagion within the individual before it can manifest as kinetic violence and political tyranny in the civic sphere. The relentless drive of porneiomachia was so firmly anchored at the heart of the Christian ethos that it continued to operate even into Protestantism's sleepwalking phase (see Sections 7.1.4 and 9.4 below).

div.head: 9.3 The Medieval Monastery — Augustinian Training Grounds
div.p: Before this introspective technology could be deployed across the general populace, it required centuries of concentrated incubation. The medieval monastery functioned as a highly controlled thermodynamic laboratory for this precise purpose. Organized around strict regulatory codes, such as the Rule of St. Benedict,See Benedict of Nursia, RB 1980: The Rule of St. Benedict in Latin and English with Notes, ed. Timothy Fry (Collegeville: Liturgical Press, 1981), chapters. 4, 7, and 48. Benedict's regulatory code institutionalizes the continuous surveillance of thoughts, the strict division of the liturgical and laboring day, and the twelve degrees of humility, establishing the foundational institutional blueprint for Western monastic discipline. monasteries were consciously engineered as protected enclaves where the Augustinian technology of introspection could be practiced continuously, safely insulated from the immediate kinetic violence of the secular E-Anna (the feudal warbands). Within these cloisters, monks developed rigorous ascetic reflexes—the precise scheduling of time, the methodical regimentation of labor, and the systematic suppression of the libido dominandi. This centuries-long experiment perfected the cultural software of internal policing. When the Protestant Reformation later dismantled the cloister walls, it did not destroy the monastic ideal; rather, it generalized these deeply ingrained cultural reflexes to the entire laity, effectively transforming the whole of society into an open-air monastery.This structural generalization was famously diagnosed by Max Weber and Charles Taylor. As Weber observed to Sebastian Franck, the Reformation meant that every Christian now had to be a monk for his entire life; see Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, trans. Talcott Parsons (London: Allen & Unwin, 1930), p. 121. See also Charles Taylor, A Secular Age (Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 2007), pp. 77-85, on the Reformation as a drive to Reform, which exported elite monastic standards of interiority and behavioral discipline to the entirety of the lay population.

div.head: 9.4 John Calvin — The Sleepwalking Eradication of the External Sovereign
div.p: This introspective technology, and its accompanying porneiomachia, reached its maximum thermodynamic efficiency during the Protestant Reformation, specifically under John Calvin. The medieval Catholic Church had maintained a hybrid system: it utilized internal policing (confession) but still relied heavily on the external, institutional Kullaba (the Papacy, the Bishops, Canon Law) to negotiate with external BDMB monarchs. Calvinism streamlined the system by declaring the absolute depravityFor Calvin's foundational formulation of radical human corruption and the bondage of the will following the Fall—later codified in Reformed orthodoxy as Total Depravity—see John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, ed. John T. McNeill, trans. Ford Lewis Battles (Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1960), Book II, chs. 1–3, pp. 241-309. of the human will, thereby demanding a state of permanent, hyper-vigilant self-surveillance against the slightest internal stirring of the E-Anna drive.

cit.quote: C'est comme un guet que Dieu a mis par-dessus l'homme, pour observer et épier tous ses secrets, afin que rien ne demeure enseveli dans les ténèbres.
It is like a watchman that God has set over man, to observe and spy out all his secrets, so that nothing may remain buried in darkness.
cit.bibl: John Calvin, Institution de la religion chrestienne (1560), IV.10.3.

cit.quote: Il nous faut faire une guerre continuelle et mortelle à notre chair, et à ses convoitises, lesquelles sont comme des bêtes sauvages qui nous veulent dévorer.
We must wage a continual and mortal war against our flesh, and against its lusts, which are like wild beasts seeking to devour us.
cit.bibl: John Calvin, Sermons sur l'Épître aux Éphésiens.

div.p: Because the Calvinist system of internal policing was so robust, the external BDMB sovereign became structurally obsolete. A society of self-policing, radically internalized Kullaba subjects does not need an E-Anna warlord to maintain cohesion; in fact, it views the transgressive, charismatic monarch as an intolerable idolatry. This is why Reformed Christianity systematically decapitated, deposed, or constitutionally neutered its monarchs (from Geneva to Cromwell’s England to the American colonies). The E-Anna was forcefully eradicated from the political sphere because the introspective Kullaba had achieved total operational supremacy. This is all the more remarkable as, by this point, Protestant Christianity was in sleepwalking mode, having lost the cultural Middle-Eastern and intertestamental keys (1 Enoch) to interpret the WoB archetype in its proper context.

div.head: 9.5 Max Weber — Diagnosing the Birth of Modernity
div.p: The sociologist Max Weber famously documented the economic and societal fallout of this psychological shift in The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism.Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, trans. Talcott Parsons (London: Allen & Unwin, 1930), pp. 98-128. Weber describes inner-worldly asceticism as the process by which monastic self-discipline was exported into the daily life of the laity, radically transforming economic behavior. Weber identified inner-worldly asceticism—the channeling of human energy away from ecstatic, martial-erotic glory (the successful societal application of porneiomachia) and into rational, methodical, and continuous labor. This is the exact thermodynamic mechanism of the Kullaba operating at scale, but in a wholly internalized fashion.

By neutralizing the E-Anna drive for zero-sum plunder and replacing it with the predictable, mathematically accountable accumulation of capital, the internalized Protestant Kullaba generated the modern world. The Liberal State and modern capitalism are the structural dividends of a population that aggressively polices its own mimetic violence. Modernity is simply the vast, bureaucratic, and rationalized architecture that emerges when the charismatic warlord is finally locked out of the system. Weber called this the iron cage of rationality—the ultimate, unbreakable glove. Ultimately, the Industrial Revolution stands as the literal, material implementation of the Neotestamental multiplying of the loaves pericopes,The miracle of the multiplication of the loaves and fishes is uniquely attested across all four canonical Gospels in six distinct pericopes: the Feeding of the Five Thousand appears in Matthew 14:13–21, Mark 6:31–44, Luke 9:10–17, and John 6:1–15, while the subsequent Feeding of the Four Thousand is recorded in Matthew 15:32–39 and Mark 8:1–9 (see also Jesus's retrospective synthesis of both events in Matthew 16:8–10 and Mark 8:18–21). understood structurally as prophecies of post-E-Anna abundance:

cit.quote: Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, he gave thanks and broke the loaves. Then he gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the people. They all ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up twelve basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over. The number of those who ate was about five thousand men, besides women and children.

div.p: By mathematically rationalizing production and directing human energy entirely away from the destructive, zero-sum game of Ishtarian plunder, the generalized Kullaba generated an unprecedented explosion of material wealth, fulfilling the Gospel's vision of near-infinite, non-violent growth through the logistics of railways, the industrial multiplication of agricultural yields, and the hygienic processing of food products at scale. As such, the New Testament can be said to contain a now-fulfilled prophecy about one of the most significant events in world history: the decrease of farm employment from above 90% down to around 3% in parallel with the establishment of near-complete food security in the Western world. Not bad for a first-century CE text written by middle-class Hellenized Jews, who were certainly not part of the intellectual elite of their day.

div.head: 9.6 Michel Foucault — The Postmodern Revolt
div.p: It is precisely the Weberian iron cage of internal policing that became the target of the late-20th-century postmodern revolt, spearheaded by Michel Foucault. Foucault dedicated his career to deconstructing what he termed pastoral power and panopticism.Michel Foucault, Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison, trans. Alan Sheridan (New York: Pantheon Books, 1977), pp. 195-228. Foucault critiques the pervasive, internalized surveillance of modern society, tracing it back to the Christian confessional. He correctly identified that the modern state controls its subjects not through spectacular violence (the E-Anna-style execution), but through the internalized, psychological discipline born of the Christian confessional's porneiomachia (the Kullaba).

However, Foucault’s critique was not a neutral, structural analysis; it was an active ideological insurgency. Foucault sought to dismantle the introspective policing mechanism specifically to liberate transgressive, erotic desire from the strictures of the porneiomachia. Viewed through the lens of the dual sovereignty framework, Foucault is the ultimate reactionary. His entire philosophical project is an elaborate excuse to tear off the Kullaba's Apollonian glove, and even its Christian internalized implementation, in order to facilitate a return to the unfettered worship of the BDMB. He hated the rational, bourgeois, self-policing society precisely because it denied him the ecstatic, boundary-breaking thrill of the ancient warband. Of course, Foucault was never honest about his actual motivations, probably not even to himself, but his personal trajectory makes them clear, as we shall see.

div.head: 9.7 Foucault's Limit-Experiences — The Girardian Critique
div.p: As René Girard predicted in Deceit, Desire, and the Novel (see Chapter 3), when the subject successfully destroys the Christian framework and abandons the internalized Kullaba, they do not achieve Rousseauian freedom. Instead, they fall instantly into the mimetic abyss. Desperate for a transcendent reality to fill the void, the subject undergoes a masochistic inversion, actively seeking out subjugation and demanding a master brutal enough to prove his own divine autonomy.

Foucault's philosophical destruction of the Christian Kullaba culminated in exactly this catastrophic, literal reality. His well-documented immersion in the sadomasochistic bathhouses of 1970s San Francisco, where he obsessively engaged as a submissive bottom, is not a peripheral biographical detail; it is the absolute empirical verification of the thermodynamic model.James Miller, The Passion of Michel Foucault (New York: Simon & Schuster, 1993), pp. 245-285. Miller details Foucault's pursuit of limit-experiences through extreme BDSM practices as the literal, physical culmination of his philosophical quest to escape the normalized, disciplinary self. Having intellectually murdered the Paternal Lawgiver and discarded the protective armor of the porneiomachia, Foucault found himself starved of ontological weight. Driven by Girardian mimetic sickness, he idolized the raw, transgressive power of the BDMB so much that he, quite literally, craved the feeling of a BD up the lower sphincter of his digestive tract.We apologize to the reader for the crassness of this expression. However, just as we deliberately employed the acronym BDMB in our conceptual overview (Section 4.2) to bypass the sanitizing veil of polite academic English, we must insist on vernacular crudity here. A clinical or philosophical phrasing would fundamentally obscure the raw, visceral, and thermodynamically desperate reality of the mimetic sickness at play. It is the ultimate tragedy of the postmodern E-Anna revival: a brilliant intellect begging a leather-clad executioner to prove to him that Sargon of Akkad is still alive.

div.head: 9.8 Vandalizing the WoB Paradigm — The Intersectional Critique of the Prophetic Tradition
div.p: Post-Foucault, the PoMo/Critical theorist crowd went on a rampage in all directions. We have seen in Section 7.1.1 that the post-war reception of the WoB was primarily driven by a Marxist/anti-imperialist framing. In recent decades, however, this consensus has been fiercely challenged by a wave of intersectional biblical scholarship that focuses explicitly on the gendered violence of the prophetic metaphor. This critique argues that the prophetic tradition’s reliance on pornographic imagery to denounce idolatry is inherently misogynistic and operates as a tool of patriarchal control.

Drorah Setel pioneered this approach by arguing that the biblical prophets' metaphorical use of female prostitution to symbolize state corruption fundamentally relies on the weaponization of shame and the patriarchal degradation of female sexuality. She asserts:

cit.quote: The prophetic metaphor of Israel as a harlot does not merely describe idolatry; it actively constructs female sexuality as inherently deviant and deserving of punishment, thereby reinforcing patriarchal control through the constant threat of public shaming.
cit.bibl: Drorah Setel, Prophets and Pornography: Female Sexual Imagery in Hosea, in Feminist Interpretation of the Bible, ed. Letty M. Russell (Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1985), p. 89.

div.p: Building upon this foundation, Gale A. Yee analyzed the broader prophetic corpus (from Hosea and Ezekiel to Revelation), arguing that the metaphorical punishment of the Whore is actually a mechanism for the ideological control of the female body. Yee notes:

cit.quote: The terrifying violence inflicted upon the metaphorical Whore by the prophetic authors serves as a disciplinary warning to actual women, utilizing the mutilated female body as a canvas upon which male authors work out their anxieties regarding political powerlessness and social boundary maintenance.
cit.bibl: Gale A. Yee, Poor Banished Children of Eve: Woman as Evil in the Hebrew Bible (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 2003), p. 112.

div.p: Julia M. O'Brien expanded this critique by applying cinema theory, asserting that the biblical texts construct a punitive Male Gaze that invites the (male) reader to revel in the voyeuristic humiliation and sexualized destruction of the offending woman. O'Brien writes:

cit.quote: The reader is positioned as the righteous male voyeur, invited to participate in the Male Gaze that simultaneously desires and punishes the hyper-sexualized Whore. The text derives a perverse, pornographic pleasure from detailing her absolute degradation.
cit.bibl: Julia M. O'Brien, Challenging Prophetic Metaphor: Theology and Ideology in the Prophets (Louisville: Westminster John Knox Press, 2008), p. 145.

div.p: Focusing directly on Revelation 17 and 18, Caroline Vander Stichele identifies the Whore of Babylon as the ultimate incarnation of the Monstrous Feminine—a grotesque, hyper-sexualized caricature engineered to evoke male castration anxiety. She concludes:

cit.quote: The Whore of Babylon is the terrifying apex of the Monstrous Feminine in biblical literature. By reducing the Roman Empire to a blood-drinking, seductive female monster who must be violently eradicated, the male author projects his profound castration anxiety onto a female figure, ultimately erasing actual female agency from the apocalyptic future.
cit.bibl: Caroline Vander Stichele, Just a Whore: The Trade in Babylon (Rev 18:3), in A Feminist Companion to the Apocalypse of John, ed. Amy-Jill Levine and Maria Mayo Robbins (London: T&T Clark, 2009), p. 72.

div.p: According to this overarching feminist consensus, the prophetic unmasking and violent destruction of the Whore is not a noble anti-imperialist critique, but rather a textual strategy designed to violently strip female agency and power from the sociopolitical landscape.

div.head: 9.9 Dismantling the Feminist Critique — The Toxic Masculinity of the BDMB
div.p: Let us first take note of the unhinged language in which the feminist critique is couched. Consider this, for example: ... the righteous male voyeur, invited to participate in the Male Gaze that simultaneously desires and punishes the hyper-sexualized Whore. Is this the expression of the calm and collected mindset of honest inquiry, or the unsettled confession-through-projection of a troubled mental universe? What about ... profound castration anxiety ...? Who is really expressing anxiety here? We have unfortunately grown accustomed to the claim that this kind of verbal onslaught deserves the qualification of scholarship. We are now going to see that the deeply questionable wording hides an absolute void of actual scholarly work.

As we have established earlier (Section 6.2, on Gilgamesh), Ishtar is not a woman. She is the symbolic projection of a deeply masculine universe—the fighting and fuckingJust like for the BDMB acronym, we are deliberately using low-register English here to avoid the inevitable dilution in meaning that higher-register language would entail. world of the rogue, the sword for hire, the gangsta-rapper. This world is perfectly understood for what it is by feminist critique, which aptly terms it toxic masculinity. Fair enough. This is exactly how the Kullaba, the authors of the Gilgamesh literature, Zarathustra, or the Parashurama Brahmins perceived the dreaded mimetic violence of the unruly band of young men. Why imagine that what we are observing here is a fight between patriarchal men and women in general? Framing the conflict in such a way is obviously an utterly anachronistic retrojection of a feature unique to our late Western culture: the so-called War Between the Sexes.The phrase War Between the Sexes became a popularized sociological idiom in the mid-20th century to describe the shifting dynamics of gender relations under modern feminism. The concept, popularized by media and literature (such as James Thurber's writings and various romantic comedies), presupposes a fundamental, systemic antagonism between men and women as broad classes. This is fundamentally alien to the institutional architecture of the ancient Near East, which operated on inter-male factional friction and elite consolidation rather than generalized gender warfare.

Yet, no Assyriologist is brave enough to point out the anachronism. A wealth of Mesopotamian sources clearly demonstrates that Inanna-Ishtar was labeled a prostitute (kar-kid in Sumerian, harīmtu in Akkadian) from her earliest textual attestations, and that her erotic and martial aspects were explicitly intertwined. In a hymn to Ishtar composed under the reign of Ammiditana of Babylon, the goddess is praised as she who causes men and women to couple while simultaneously holding the power of kingship, the power of dominion.Benjamin R. Foster, Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature (Bethesda: CDL Press, 2005), pp. 71-73. A Sumerian hymn explicitly connects her martial ferocity to her promiscuity:

cit.quote: My father gave me the heavens, gave me the earth... I am the hierodule (kar-kid) in heaven, the hierodule on earth.
cit.bibl: Martha T. Roth, The Prostitute and the Prophet in Ancient Near Eastern Culture, in Prostitution and Religion, ed. K. van der Toorn (Leiden: Brill, 1998), pp. 21-38.

div.p: As Martha Roth notes, the divine designation of prostitute was an authentic Mesopotamian theological category, not a later prophetic invention.

Further primary sources continuously reinforce this explicit connection between Inanna-Ishtar's martial supremacy and her identity as a prostitute or patroness of the tavern. A Sumerian hymn dedicated to Inanna (Inana C) boldly declares:

cit.quote: When I sit in the alehouse, I am a woman, and I am an exuberant young man. When I am present at a place of quarreling, I am the woman who understands the matter. When I sit by the gate of the tavern, I am a prostitute familiar with the penis; the friend of a man, the girlfriend of a woman.
cit.bibl: Jeremy Black, Graham Cunningham, Eleanor Robson, and Gábor Zólyomi, A cir-namcub to Inana (Inana C), in The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (Oxford: University of Oxford, 1998), lines 16-22.

div.p: In another text, Iddin-Dagan A, the goddess's orgiastic festival is described as the explicit locus of her martial and sovereign power, where young men deliberately blur gender boundaries to honor her:

cit.quote: The people of Sumer parade before you... The young men who carry weapons before you, who carry the throw-stick and the shield before you, who play the lyre and the tambourine before you... they perform the head-over-heels dance for you.
cit.bibl: Jeremy Black, Graham Cunningham, Eleanor Robson, and Gábor Zólyomi, A praise poem of Iddin-Dagan (Iddin-Dagan A), in The Electronic Text Corpus of Sumerian Literature (Oxford: University of Oxford, 1998), lines 44-53.

div.p: Finally, a Neo-Assyrian oracle addressed to King Esarhaddon seamlessly fuses her identity as a fierce warrior with her erotic, physical embrace of the sovereign:

cit.quote: I am Ishtar of Arbela. O Esarhaddon, king of Assyria... I will flay your enemies and give them to you. I am Ishtar of Arbela. In the chamber of the bed, I am your beloved.
cit.bibl: Simo Parpola, Assyrian Prophecies, State Archives of Assyria, Vol. 9 (Helsinki: Helsinki University Press, 1997), Text 1.1.

div.p: The most explicit link between the martial and erotic domains of Inanna-Ishtar is found not just in a single story, but in the very language used to describe her actions. Both the Sumerian word ešen and the Akkadian word mēlulu translate roughly to play or dance. In Mesopotamian literature, this specific play is used interchangeably as a euphemism for two things: sexual intercourse and physical combat. In love poetry, Dumuzi (her consort) is invited to partake in her ešen (sexual play). In war poetry, the battlefield is repeatedly referred to as the Dance of Inanna or the Playground of Ishtar. To engage in mortal combat was to participate in her terrifying, ecstatic dance.For the linguistic conflation of sexual intercourse and battle through the terminology of play and dance (ešen or ešemen in Sumerian, and mēlulu in Akkadian), see Rivkah Harris, Inanna-Ishtar as Paradox and a Coincidence of Opposites, History of Religions 30, no. 3 (1991): 261-278. Harris explores how the goddess's volatile nature unifies these extremes, noting that the texts explicitly identify battle as the dance of Inanna. See also Gwendolyn Leick, Sex and Eroticism in Mesopotamian Literature (London: Routledge, 1994), pp. 64-65, which details how the play of the goddess seamlessly bridges the realms of the bedchamber and lethal combat.

So whose male gaze are we talking about here? That of the patriarchal Kullaba or that of the rape-prone E-Anna warband? Whose monstrous feminine are we talking about? The complete silence on these questions from the ranks of the intersectional theorists exposes their scholarship for what it is: shallow journalistic propaganda.

Furthermore, it was the Kullaba side of Mesopotamian culture that was genuinely concerned with sexual violence and legislated against it. The Code of Ur-Nammu and the Code of Hammurabi both contain explicit provisions protecting virgin women from rape, demonstrating that the patriarchal state apparatus sought to suppress the very sexual chaos that the warband embodied.See Martha T. Roth, Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor (Atlanta: Scholars Press, 1995), Laws of Ur-Nammu §7 and Laws of Hammurabi §130. There is therefore ample evidence that Ishtar-Inanna, the archetype of the Whore of Babylon, was intimately linked with leaders of rape-prone armies, like Sargon of Akkad, while the anti-rape party was that of the patriarchal Kullaba. Furthermore, John of Patmos obviously knew of all this because of Nahum's indictment of Nineveh in explicitly anti-Ishtar language.Nahum 3:4-5. Nahum directly indicts Nineveh: Because of the multitude of the harlotries of the well-favored harlot, the mistress of sorceries, who sells nations through her harlotries. This prophetic language is a direct, structural critique of the Assyrian state's reliance on the Ishtarian charismatic engine. The existence of this material, including the consistent association of Ishtar with prostitution in ancient texts, directly contradicts the attempts of feminist hermeneutics of Revelation to read a specifically patriarchal pornographic male gaze into it.Even within mainstream biblical scholarship, the methodological flaws and anachronisms of the pornoprophetic school have drawn pointed criticism. Andrew Sloane demonstrates that reading prophetic harlotry imagery through the lens of modern pornography and voyeuristic male gaze theory fundamentally distorts the rhetorical and theological function of these texts, which were designed to provoke covenantal horror rather than erotic arousal; see Andrew Sloane, Aberrant Textuality? The Case of Ezekiel the (Porno) Prophet, Tyndale Bulletin 59, no. 1 (2008): 53-76. Similarly, Sharon Moughtin-Mumby critiques the reductive feminist assumption of a monolithic, literalized marriage metaphor, showing how such readings flatten complex, context-specific rhetorical attacks on political and cultic apostasy; see Sharon Moughtin-Mumby, Sexual and Marital Metaphors in Hosea, Jeremiah, Isaiah, and Ezekiel (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2008), pp. 1-30. For a parallel critique of applying reductive gender binaries to the Whore of Babylon in Revelation 17–18, demonstrating that the figure targets imperial politico-economic seduction rather than actual women, see Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza, The Book of Revelation: Justice and Judgment, 2nd ed. (Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1998), pp. 210-226. Yet, why does it persist? We will attempt to answer this question in the next section.

Before we do that, let us go back to actual historical scholarship for a brief moment. As we have amply illustrated in a long series of examples in Chapters 4 through 8, the structural friction animating ancient history is not a war between Patriarchy and women. It is the existential, institutional conflict between the Kullaba and the E-Anna—between the senatus (the elder council, rooted in law, deliberation, and linguistic trust) and the juventusIn classical Latin historiography, senatus (derived from senex, old man) and juventus (the collective body of military-age young men, cognate with the goddess Juventas) frequently operate as structurally opposed sociopolitical poles. Titus Livius (Livy) repeatedly frames the internal convulsions of the early Roman Republic as a generational and institutional clash between the sober, legalistic restraint of the seniores in the Senate and the volatile, war-hungry, or seditious impulses of the juventus (especially the patrician youth who nostalgically favored the Tarquinian monarchy); see Titus Livius, Ab Urbe Condita, trans. B. O. Foster (Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1919), 2.3–4, 2.28–30, and 3.11–15. Similarly, Sallust diagnoses the terminal collapse of the Republic in the Bellum Catilinae by detailing how the rogue aristocrat Catiline specifically targeted and mobilized the Roman juventus—corrupting them through luxury, debt, and illicit erotic entanglements—to forge a fanatical, transgressive warband aimed at slaughtering the senatus; see Sallust, The War with Catiline. The War with Jugurtha, trans. J. C. Rolfe, Loeb Classical Library 116 (Cambridge: Harvard University Press, 1921), chs. 14–16 and 37–38. As Georges Dumézil demonstrated, this Latin binary preserves the archaic Indo-European tension between the First Function elders and the Second Function ✶kóryos brotherhood. (the martial warband, fueled by excess testosterone, territorial aggression, and mimetic frenzy). The Ishtarian goddess is the ideological patron of this rape-prone, violent warband, arrayed behind their bombastic BDMB leader. Her erotic allure is not female agency. It is the mimetic gravitational pull that mesmerizes the young warrior and paralyzes civic opposition. Furthermore, Inanna is in fact a self-declared whore, if we are to trust the poetry of another feminist icon, Enheduanna.A glaring ideological contradiction splits contemporary feminist engagement with the ancient Near East. While feminist biblical scholars vehemently lambast the Hebrew prophets and John of Patmos for their pornoprophetic attacks on the Whore of Babylon, feminist art historians and Assyriologists—most notably Zainab Bahrani—simultaneously celebrate her direct Mesopotamian prototype, Inanna-Ishtar, along with her chief imperial propagandist Enheduanna. In Women of Babylon, Bahrani explicitly rehabilitates Ishtar's transgressive, hyper-sexualized, and violent persona, framing her as a subversive, boundary-breaking figure of unbridled female autonomy—effectively retrojecting a modern, Hollywood-style strong independent woman trope onto antiquity; see Zainab Bahrani, Women of Babylon: Gender and Representation in Mesopotamia (London: Routledge, 2001), pp. 141-160. By romanticizing the exact deity whose historical function was to sanctify Sargon's standing army and fuel the mimetic frenzy of the warband, feminist scholarship inadvertently gives its enthusiastic blessing to the supreme ancient patroness of toxic masculinity. Therefore, the prophetic pornographic critique is not an attack on the female body, but a deliberate, surgical unmasking of the state's erotic-martial engine. By exposing the self-declared whore’s nakedness and stripping away her luxurious theatricality, the prophet breaks the mimetic spell of the BDMB's seductive propaganda, revealing the brutal, rapacious war machine hidden beneath. The biblical prophetic and apostolic critique of the E-Anna is the most effective condemnation of Toxic Masculinity ever put to writing. Why most effective? Because instead of being motivated by secret envy (see below), it stems from genuine repentance: the sincere desire to turn away from the temptation of the martial-erotic goddess and her never-ending promises of triumphant pride. This call to repentance is addressed to men: the men of the juventus whom she could tempt into mistreating, among others, women.

By inviting the E-Anna back into religious-societal discourse, intersectional critical theory is endangering all the oppressed categories it vows to protect by unwittingly validating the worst possible oppressor, the toxic BDMB. Nowhere is this more visible than in the black impoverished neighborhoods where the worst menace faced by residents is not the white man, but the local drug lord with his gangsta-rapper persona. In this context, the Ishtar-fueled BDMB is back at the center of society.

div.head: 9.10 The Current Religious Landscape
div.p: We asked above why it is that the defective scholarship described above persists and even tends to increase in influence. The answer to this question is that intersectional critique only has the appearance of scholarship. In fact, it is a form of apologetics for a rogue, unacknowledged religion. This religion may be called Female-Centric Nietzschean Self-Worship (FCNSW). Nietzsche was famously misogynistic, but this is by no means an obstacle. On the contrary, FCNSW is disguised male-worship. No need for Freudian Penis Envy here.Freudian Penis Envy posits a biological deficit at the core of female psychology. In the Girardian framework, however, the envy is strictly mimetic—it is the desire to possess the ontological weight and charismatic autonomy perceived in the hyper-masculine BDMB mediator, having nothing to do with literal anatomy. The Nietzschean Übermensch was initially, and almost immediately, received in the wider context of Western culture as Male-Centric Nietzschean Self-Worship (MCNSW), which gave us the SS and the attendant mid-20th-century horrors. Its female version, FCNSW, is simply Girardian mimetic desire for the fantasized MCNSW-constructed Übermensch. As René Girard pointed out in Deceit, Desire, and the Novel, in the world of the Black, where overt idolatry is no longer possible, the impulse towards the mediator can only turn into the most intense hatred.René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel: Self and Other in Literary Structure, trans. Yvonne Freccero (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1965), p. 41. Girard observes: The subject is torn between two opposite feelings toward his model—the most submissive reverence and the most intense malice. This is the passion we call hatred. It is this hatred-laced metaphysical desire that the language of the quotations highlighted in the first paragraph of the previous section expresses. Like Catholicism, FCNSW has its inquisition, which can deprive those who challenge it of their professional reputation and livelihood (sometimes their freedom). The persistent spread of propagandistic-journalistic feminist critical scholarship in academia (where it consistently violates all norms of actual scholarship) and in the media is a testament to the intimidation power of this inquisitorial apparatus.

One recent illustration of the potency of FCNSW as a popular religion is the cult-like following of the Fifty Shades of Grey franchise. This business conglomerate sold over 165 million books and 150 million cinema tickets to primarily female buyers who thus took part in the biggest-ever virtual pilgrimage (far bigger than the Hindu Kumbh MelaThe Maha Kumbh Mela is widely recognized as the largest peaceful religious gathering in human history, with modern festivals drawing an estimated 120 to 150 million pilgrims over a span of several weeks. See Kama Maclean, Pilgrimage and Power: The Kumbh Mela in Allahabad, 1765-1954 (New York: Oxford University Press, 2008), pp. 3-15. The fact that the commercial metrics of the Fifty Shades phenomenon outstrip even these staggering physical congregations underscores its unprecedented scale as a decentralized, globalized mimetic event.) honoring the goddess and her male double, Christian Grey. The BDSM element in this religious celebration was also predicted by René Girard. In Deceit, Desire, and the Novel, Girard demonstrates that when the subject's project of self-deification (frustrated mastery) inevitably collapses into inner emptiness, the subject undergoes a masochistic inversion. Desperate to locate a transcendent reality to fill the void, the subject actively seeks out subjugation, demanding an ever more cruel master whose capacity to inflict pain seems to guarantee his unshakeable, divine autonomy, as we have seen with Foucault. Girard explicitly diagnoses this search for the real god (who, in this modern context, takes the form of the MCNSW Übermensch, i.e., toxic masculinity):

cit.quote: The subject turns toward the only master who can still fascinate him, the one who makes him suffer. [...] The masochist asks his executioner to prove to him that he is a god.
cit.bibl: René Girard, Deceit, Desire, and the Novel: Self and Other in Literary Structure, trans. Yvonne Freccero (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins Press, 1965), pp. 176, 178.

div.p: In the context of the FCNSW phenomenon, when the female subject's own pursuit of autonomous deification rings hollow, she mimetically conjures the absolute, sadistic dominance of the BDMB billionaire to forcefully reinstate the ontological weight she lacks.

div.head: 9.11 The Irresistible Attraction of the Frat Sex Ritual II
div.p: With the entirety of this macro-historical and psychological architecture laid bare, the underlying forces that drew Jane Doe into the Chi Phi fraternity house on the Cornell campus on that October night become crystal clear. At the foundational level, we are witnessing the enduring, millennia-old gravitational pull of the Ishtar-fueled BDMB (the frat Legend) and the archaic PIE ✶kóryos warband arrayed around him. Despite centuries of Kullaba institutionalization and Christian porneiomachia, the primal mimetic engine of the E-Anna has survived, preserved within the amber of Anglo-American elite subculture and democratized into the collegiate McThelema. By crossing the threshold of the fraternity house, the female participant steps directly into an ancient liturgical space designed to consecrate the young alpha male and his homosocial brotherhood through collective, boundary-shattering sexual transgression.

Yet, as our excursion through modern Girardian pathology demonstrates, there is something far darker and more urgent at work in the contemporary iteration of this rite. Because we now inhabit the world of the Black—a post-Christian landscape where the internal Kullaba has been systematically demolished by the postmodern revolt, while overt idolatry remains socially taboo—the attraction of the clandestine hieros gamos is exponentially multiplied by the demonic aura of the terminal Girardian masochistic phase. In the 10th-century Volga ritual documented by Ibn Fadlan (Section 5.4.8), it was a disenfranchised slave girl who was subjected to communal intercourse and sacrificed to accompany the Rus chieftain. In the modern collegiate McThelema, no slave girl is needed; instead, it is the patrician daughter of a nearby elite sorority who voluntarily walks up to the altar, offering herself in an orgiastic act of reputational suicide.

Ultimately, the campus Stacy and the middle-class housewife are trapped in the exact same ontological vacuum. Having been indoctrinated since youth into the dogmas of autonomous self-deification (FCNSW), the young elite woman inevitably discovers that the promised divinity of the sovereign self is a mirage. Crushed by the resulting existential emptiness—and surrounded by sorority peers operating in the ruthless, hyper-competitive panopticon of the Black—she undergoes the classic masochistic inversion. Just like Foucault and the tens of millions of FCNSW consumer-worshippers flocking to the virtual Fifty Shades pilgrimage, the upper-class sorority girl simply cannot resist the gravitational pull of the MCNSW Moloch Übermensch. She seeks out the most callous, high-status fraternity BDMBs precisely because their collective, degrading consumption of her body—and the guaranteed social annihilation that follows—is the only force brutal enough to shatter her numbness and prove to her that a god still exists.
